unit_label: Module C unit 1 (courseware unit 17), part 2: pricing of advances (MCLR, external benchmark, spread, reset, exemptions)

facts.statement: A bank charges interest on loans in accordance with the Directions; there must be a comprehensive interest rate policy approved by the Board or a committee of the Board, including the pricing of microfinance loans. All floating rate loans other than the exempted ones are priced with reference to a benchmark; a bank is free to offer all categories of advances on fixed or floating rates; for floating rate advances the actual lending rate is the reference benchmark plus the components of spread; the reference benchmark must form part of the loan contract; there can be no lending below the benchmark rate for a particular maturity for loans linked to that benchmark; interest on advances is charged at monthly rests (with different treatment of some agricultural advances) and rounded off to the nearest rupee; interest on small value loans such as personal loans must be justifiable having regard to the total cost incurred by the bank and the return reasonably expected. Interest rates on fixed rate loans of tenor below three years may not be less than the benchmark rate for similar tenor.

The Base Rate (an internal benchmark for floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed between 1 July 2010 and 31 March 2016) includes the elements of lending rates common to all categories of borrowers; there is only one Base Rate for each bank; a bank reviews it at least once a quarter with Board or ALCO approval. The Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR) is the internal benchmark for floating rate rupee loans sanctioned and renewed from 1 April 2016 (subject to the external benchmark provisions). Existing loans linked to the Base Rate or BPLR continue till repayment or renewal, and borrowers have the option to move to MCLR-linked loans on mutually acceptable terms without it being treated as foreclosure.

The MCLR comprises four components: marginal cost of funds (marginal cost of borrowings and return on net worth), negative carry on account of CRR, operating costs and tenor premium. Negative carry on the mandatory CRR, which arises because CRR balances earn no return, is calculated as Required CRR x (marginal cost) / (1 - CRR), using the marginal cost of funds. Operating costs cover all costs associated with providing the loan product including the cost of raising funds, but exclude costs of services separately recovered through service charges, and are calculated as a percentage of the marginal cost of funds. The tenor premium arises from loan commitments with longer tenor, must be uniform for all types of loans for a given residual tenor, and is for the residual period up to the next reset date.

The tenor of the MCLR corresponds to the tenor of the funds in the single largest maturity bucket if that bucket is more than 30 per cent of the funds other than equity; if no single bucket exceeds 30 per cent, it corresponds to the weighted average tenor of the two or more buckets, taken in descending order of maturity, that together account for more than 30 per cent of the funds (the Directions illustrate with buckets of 15.1, 11.8 and 9.3 per cent for maturities of 5 years and above, 3 to under 5 years, and 2 to under 3 years, whose cumulative weight of 36.2 per cent exceeds 30 per cent, so the MCLR corresponds to the weighted average tenor of the first three buckets). Because MCLR is tenor linked, a bank arrives at the MCLR of each maturity by adding the tenor premium or discount to the sum of the marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR and operating costs, and publishes the overnight, one-month, three-month, six-month and one-year MCLR (with the option of longer maturities). A bank reviews and publishes its MCLR of different maturities every month on a pre-announced date with Board or delegated committee approval.

All floating rate personal or retail loans (housing, auto and so on) and floating rate loans to micro, small and medium enterprises are benchmarked to an External Benchmark Rate; a bank may offer external benchmark linked loans to other borrowers too; and, for transparency, a bank must adopt a uniform external benchmark within a loan category, so multiple benchmarks within one loan category are not allowed. The external benchmark rate includes the RBI policy repo rate, the Government of India three-month and six-month Treasury Bill yields published by Financial Benchmarks India Private Ltd (FBIL), or any other benchmark market interest rate published by FBIL. The interest rate under an external benchmark is reset at least once in three months. The courseware says the review and publication requirement for MCLR does not apply to external benchmarks because banks have no influence over them, which is why such loans transmit policy rates in a non-interventionist manner.
facts.locator: RBI_IRA_2025 paragraphs 25-27, 38 and the definition of external benchmark rate; courseware printed pp. 411-413

facts.statement: A bank must have a Board-approved policy delineating the components of spread, which sets principles to determine the quantum of each component, the range of spread for a given category of borrower or type of loan, and the delegation of powers in loan pricing. Under MCLR the broad components of spread are business strategy (business strategy, market competition, embedded options in the loan product, market liquidity of the loan) and credit risk premium (representing the default risk of the loan, arrived at from an appropriate credit risk rating or scoring model, customer relationship, expected losses and collaterals); both components are either positive or zero and cannot be negative. The spread charged to an existing borrower may not be increased except on account of deterioration in the credit risk profile of the customer, supported by a full-fledged risk profile review; this does not apply to loans under consortium or multiple banking arrangements. Under an external benchmark a bank is free to decide the spread, but the credit risk premium may change only when the borrower's credit assessment undergoes a substantial change, as agreed in the loan contract; other components including operating cost may be altered once in three years, though they may be reduced earlier for customer retention on justifiable grounds in a non-discriminatory manner under the bank's policy.
facts.locator: RBI_IRA_2025 paragraphs 28 and 30-33; courseware printed pp. 411-412

facts.statement: Under MCLR a bank may link reset dates either to the date of first disbursement of the loan or limit or to the date of review of the MCLR; the MCLR prevailing on the date of first disbursement (partial or full) applies till the next reset date irrespective of changes in the benchmark in the interim; the periodicity of reset is one year or lower, forms part of the loan contract, and corresponds to the tenor of the MCLR to which the loan is linked. Existing loans linked to the MCLR, Base Rate or BPLR continue till repayment or renewal; floating rate term loans for borrowers eligible to prepay without prepayment charges are eligible to switch to an external benchmark without any charges or fees except reasonable administrative and legal costs, at the rate a new loan of the same category, type, tenor and amount would carry, and other existing borrowers have the option to move on mutually acceptable terms; a switch-over is not treated as foreclosure.
facts.locator: RBI_IRA_2025 paragraphs 34-37 and 40-41; courseware printed p. 413

facts.statement: Exempted from the benchmark provisions: loans covered by Government of India schemes under which the bank must charge the scheme rate; working capital term loans and funded interest term loans granted as part of a rectification or restructuring package; loans under government refinance schemes at prescribed rates (to the extent refinance is available, the uncovered part following the benchmark guidelines); advances against the bank's own deposits, advances to the bank's own employees including retired employees, advances to the chief executive officer or whole time directors, loans linked to a market determined external benchmark, and fixed rate loans of tenor above three years (for hybrid loans the floating portion follows the floating rate instructions); and fixed rate loans (and the fixed portion of hybrid loans) of tenor up to three years, other than bill discounting and factoring, may not be priced below the sum of marginal cost of funds, negative carry on CRR, operating cost and the tenor premium for the corresponding maturity on the date of sanction. For advances in foreign currency a bank has the freedom to set rates under its Board-approved policy, with reference to a market determined external benchmark plus spread.

payload.title: The rules of pricing a floating rate loan
payload.core_explanation_md:
RBI requires every bank to have a **Board-approved interest rate policy**. The rules that run through the Directions:

- A floating rate loan is priced as **reference benchmark + spread**.
- The benchmark used is written into the **loan contract**.
- **No lending below the benchmark** for that maturity.
- Banks can offer **fixed or floating** rates on any category of advance.
- **Fixed rate loans of under three years** may not be priced below the benchmark rate for similar tenor.
- Interest is charged at **monthly rests** (some agricultural advances follow other rules) and **rounded to the nearest rupee**.
- Interest on **small value loans** such as personal loans must be **justifiable** against the bank's cost and a reasonable return.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: This replaces the older 2016 text that the courseware reproduces; the structure is the same.

self_check.prompt_text: How is the lending rate on a floating rate loan arrived at?
self_check.expected_takeaway: By adding the components of spread to the reference benchmark rate written into the loan contract.

payload.title: From Base Rate to MCLR
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Benchmark | Applied to | Key feature |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **BPLR** | Older loans | Continues till repayment or renewal |
| **Base Rate** | Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed **1 July 2010 to 31 March 2016** | Elements **common to all borrowers**; **one** per bank; reviewed at least **quarterly** |
| **MCLR** | Floating rate rupee loans sanctioned or renewed **from 1 April 2016** | Internal benchmark built from the bank's **marginal** cost |

Existing borrowers on Base Rate or BPLR may **move to MCLR** on mutually acceptable terms, and the switch is **not a foreclosure**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The Base Rate was based on average or marginal cost; the MCLR moved to a marginal-cost basis so that policy rate changes pass through faster.

self_check.prompt_text: From which date are floating rate rupee loans priced with reference to MCLR?

payload.title: The four building blocks of MCLR
payload.core_explanation_md:
| Component | What it is |
| --- | --- |
| **Marginal cost of funds** | Marginal cost of **borrowings** plus **return on net worth** |
| **Negative carry on CRR** | The cost of holding the mandatory CRR, which earns **nothing**: **CRR x marginal cost / (1 - CRR)** |
| **Operating costs** | All costs of providing the loan product incl. cost of raising funds; **excludes** costs recovered through separate service charges; set as a **percentage of the marginal cost of funds** |
| **Tenor premium** | Extra for longer commitments; **uniform** for all loans of a given residual tenor; covers the period to the next reset |

**MCLR = marginal cost + negative carry on CRR + operating costs + tenor premium.**

Why the CRR formula divides by (1 - CRR): for every rupee the bank raises, only (1 - CRR) can be lent, so the cost of the idle CRR portion is spread over the lendable amount.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Because the tenor premium differs by tenor, the bank gets a different MCLR for each maturity.

self_check.prompt_text: Which MCLR component is the same for all loans of a given residual tenor, whoever the borrower is?

payload.title: Which tenor does the MCLR cover, and when is it published?
payload.core_explanation_md:
The bank's funds (other than equity) are grouped into **maturity buckets**.

- If the **single largest bucket** is **more than 30 per cent**, the MCLR corresponds to **that bucket's tenor**.
- Otherwise, take buckets **in descending order of maturity** until their cumulative weight is **more than 30 per cent**, and use the **weighted average tenor** of those buckets.

**Illustration (from the Directions):** buckets of 15.1 (5 years and above), 11.8 (3 to under 5 years), 9.3 (2 to under 3 years) and so on. No bucket exceeds 30 per cent; the first two total 26.9, still under 30; adding the third gives **36.2**, so the MCLR corresponds to the **weighted average tenor of the first three buckets**.

**Publication:** the bank publishes **overnight, one-month, three-month, six-month and one-year** MCLR (longer maturities optional), reviewed **every month** on a **pre-announced date** with Board or delegated committee approval.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The idea is that the headline MCLR should reflect where most of the bank's funding really sits.

self_check.prompt_text: How often must a bank review and publish its MCLR?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Every month, on a pre-announced date.

payload.title: External benchmark lending
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Compare MCLR: the bank builds and publishes it; an external benchmark is simply taken from an outside source.

self_check.prompt_text: May a bank use two different external benchmarks for housing loans?

payload.title: Spread: what it holds and when it may change
payload.core_explanation_md:
A bank needs a **Board-approved spread policy** saying how to fix each component, the **range** of spread for each borrower category or loan type, and who may decide pricing.

| | **Under MCLR** | **Under an external benchmark** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Components | **Business strategy** + **credit risk premium** (both **zero or positive**, never negative) | Bank is **free** to decide the spread |
| Raising spread on an existing borrower | Only for **deterioration in credit risk**, backed by a **full risk profile review** (not for consortium loans) | **Credit risk premium** may change only on a **substantial change** in credit assessment, as agreed in the contract |
| Other components (including operating cost) | n/a | May be altered **once in three years**; may be **reduced earlier** for retention, on justifiable, non-discriminatory grounds |

**Credit risk premium** reflects the loan's default risk, from a rating or scoring model, the customer relationship, expected losses and collaterals.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The rule protects the borrower: a bank cannot raise the spread merely because it would like more margin.

self_check.prompt_text: Can the spread components under MCLR be negative?
self_check.expected_takeaway: No: they must be zero or positive.

payload.title: Reset of rates, switching, and the loans that are exempt
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Reset under MCLR:** the bank may link reset dates to the **first disbursement** or to the **MCLR review date**. The MCLR on the date of first disbursement applies **until the next reset date**, whatever happens to the benchmark meanwhile. Reset periodicity is **one year or lower**, written into the contract, and matches the **tenor of the MCLR** the loan is linked to.

**Switching to an external benchmark:** existing loans continue till repayment or renewal. A floating rate term loan whose borrower may **prepay without charge** can switch **without charges or fees** (except reasonable administrative and legal costs), at the **rate a new loan of the same category, type, tenor and amount would get**. Others may move on **mutually acceptable terms**. A switch is **not a foreclosure**.

**Exempt from the benchmark rules:** government scheme loans at scheme rates; **working capital term loans and funded interest term loans** in a restructuring; refinance-scheme loans (to the extent of refinance); advances against **own deposits**, to **own employees** (including retired), to the **CEO or whole time directors**; loans linked to a market-determined external benchmark; and **fixed rate loans above three years**. Fixed rate loans of **up to three years** (except bill discounting and factoring) may not be below marginal cost + negative carry on CRR + operating cost + tenor premium.

**Foreign currency advances:** a market-determined external benchmark plus spread, under the Board policy.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The floor for short fixed rate loans means banks cannot lend fixed below their own cost-based benchmark.

self_check.prompt_text: Which kind of restructuring loan is exempt from the benchmark rules?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Working capital term loans and funded interest term loans granted as part of a rectification or restructuring package.

payload.title: Building an MCLR and a lending rate
payload.core_explanation_md: A bank has a marginal cost of funds of 8.00 per cent, a required CRR of 4 per cent, operating costs of 0.50 per cent and a tenor premium of 0.20 per cent for one year. Its spread for a customer is 0.40 per cent business strategy and 0.60 per cent credit risk premium. Find the one-year MCLR and the customer's rate.

Spread: both components zero or positive.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Zero, because no funds would be held idle.

unresolved: The courseware (printed pp. 410 to 413) reproduces the 2016 Interest Rate on Advances Directions as updated on 12 September 2023. Those have been replaced by the Reserve Bank of India (Commercial Banks - Interest Rates on Advances) Directions, 2025 of 28 November 2025, which were read in full (20 pages) and are the basis of every fact here. The copy is the 28 November 2025 text; amendments after that date were not searched for.

The courseware gives dates for the external benchmark requirement (micro and small enterprises from 1 October 2019 and medium enterprises from 1 April 2020); the 2025 Directions require floating rate retail and MSME loans to be benchmarked to an external benchmark without those dates, so the dates are not taught.

The courseware's description of reset and spread conditions matches the 2025 text in all points used. The courseware on printed p. 413 continues with treatment of existing borrowers and periodicity of charging interest; the agricultural interest provisions of paragraph 6(7) are summarised only as "different rests for some agricultural advances" and no amounts are taught.
